LESSON 91 OF 106·Defensive Operations: Detect, Respond, Recover

SIEM, Alerts and Tuning Out Noise

How a detection becomes a decision: what alerting is for, why an untrusted alert is worse than none, and how tuning turns a rule from a hypothesis into a piece of evidence.

Applied Foundation2 min
Why this matters

A SIEM collects everything and therefore alerts on whatever someone configured. The work is deciding what deserves a human, and the honest answer is usually a small fraction of what fires.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

  1. Source: A detection rule encodes a hypothesis about attacker behaviour, and its quality is the quality of that hypothesis.
  2. Boundary: The system processes well-formed input along the intended happy path.
  3. Outcome: State transitions and responses remain within expected operational bounds.

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.
  2. Weakness: Check how many alerts are open, how old they are, and how many were true positives.
  3. Impact: The component trusts unverified data, crossing a confidentiality or integrity boundary.
01 Untrusted Input

02 Server Policy Gate
Verified
03 Verified Operation
  1. Verification: Measure coverage against a behaviour framework, so gaps are visible rather than assumed absent.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • check how many alerts are open, how old they are, and how many were true positives
  • check whether each alert has a documented first action, and who performs it
  • check which attacker techniques you have any coverage for at all
  • check how long a real alert took to reach a responder, measured rather than estimated

How it works

  • A detection rule encodes a hypothesis about attacker behaviour, and its quality is the quality of that hypothesis.
  • A rule that fires on common activity produces alert fatigue, and alert fatigue is functionally the same as no detection.
  • Coverage should be measured against known techniques rather than against the number of rules deployed.
  • Tuning is continuous: an environment baseline changes, so a rule that was rare becomes common.
  • The measure that matters is how long a true positive takes to reach a person who can act.

The background

  • Early correlation engines were log-file filters that produced little more than grep with a schedule.
  • Rules migrated into platforms as regular expressions, which made detection easy to write and hard to maintain.
  • The volume of alerts became the dominant problem, and organisations started measuring false positive rates deliberately.
  • Detection engineering and behaviour analytics moved the goal from more rules to more coverage.

Real-world examples

  • A queue with thousands of open alerts is read by nobody, and the rule is present on a compliance slide.
  • A rule written for a specific incident and never generalised catches that incident once.
  • An alert with no documented response is a notification, and notifications do not reduce risk.

What to look for

  • Check how many alerts are open, how old they are, and how many were true positives.
  • Check whether each alert has a documented first action, and who performs it.
  • Check which attacker techniques you have any coverage for at all.
  • Check how long a real alert took to reach a responder, measured rather than estimated.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

MITRE ATT&CK — Detection Strategies

Reading the named approaches for turning observed adversary behaviour into a detection, and comparing them against the categories your own rules actually fall into

Open MITRE resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Measure coverage against a behaviour framework, so gaps are visible rather than assumed absent.
  • Give every alert a documented first action, and delete the ones that have none.
  • Tune continuously using the false positive data you already generate, rather than in a one-off project.
  • Prioritise alerts by the technique they indicate, so triage starts from impact.
  • Track time to detect and time to respond as the primary metrics, since they predict outcome better than rule count.
